articlePath.lede.defaultMessage: Five rungs, tried in order; the first that answers wins. The snapshot built into the app comes first, because the promise is that an article opens without Wi-Fi. The cache behind the second and the fifth rung has three limits. What reaches the screen is one string, handed to a WebView.
articlePath.lede.description: The paragraph under that heading. A rung is this drawing’s own word for one step of the cascade in packages/app-core/src/articles/load.ts.

articlePath.title.description: The drawing’s name, as the heading of its own page and on the card that opens it.

components.alsoExported.description: The heading over what a folder’s files export beside their components: helpers, constants, sample data.

components.barrel.defaultMessage: This folder has a barrel, so a caller names the folder and not the file.
components.barrel.description: Behind the ⓘ beside the import line of a folder that has an index file re-exporting its components. A “barrel” is the index file; the line above it shows the import a caller writes.

components.card.bundle.description: A badge on a card whose component this site cannot draw itself. It states where the drawing happens rather than reporting a failure: the component’s own page frames the app and draws it there.

components.card.bundleNote.defaultMessage: Its page draws it in the shipped app.
components.card.bundleNote.description: The line under that badge when no more specific reason is recorded for this component in components/direct-ids.ts.

components.card.clipped.description: Printed over the lower edge of a card that cannot show the whole of its component. {height} is the component’s real height in CSS pixels, measured in the browser. Read by eye only: the same fact is in the accessible name of the link over the drawing, components.card.specimens.clipped.

components.card.noDoc.description: Stands in where a component’s source carries no prose to print. reference.symbol.noDoc says the same thing about a symbol on /reference.

components.card.props.description: The count in a card’s bottom-right corner. {count} is how many props the component takes, and may be zero.

components.card.specimens.description: The accessible name of the link covering a card’s drawing, which opens that component’s own page. {name} is the component’s name in the source, such as SectionCard, and is not translated. components.card.specimens.clipped is the same link when the card is cutting the component off.

components.card.specimens.clipped.defaultMessage: Every specimen of {name}, which this card clips at {height} px
components.card.specimens.clipped.description: The same link as components.card.specimens, on a card that cannot show the whole component. {name} is the component’s name in the source and is not translated; {height} is the component’s real height in CSS pixels. It carries the fact that the note over the drawing states visually, because that note is hidden from a screen reader.

components.detail.breadcrumb.description: Read aloud as the name of the trail above the drawing, and never drawn. The trail itself is the components page, the folder, and this component.

components.detail.crumb.description: The first step of that trail, which is the name of the page it links to. components.title is that page’s own heading and reads the same in English; the two move together and are two entries because one is a heading and one is a link in a trail.

components.detail.device.description: The label over the select that picks the size the app is framed at. frame.device is the same word on the preview’s own bar, where it is read aloud rather than drawn.

components.detail.drawnBy.description: Read aloud as the group name of the switch between the two renderings, and NEVER drawn: `ui/kit/segmented.tsx` hides a legend unless `showLegend` is passed, and this one does not pass it. The heading a reader sees over the switch is shell.section.rendering. So the two options below have to stand on their own, and a translation that made them agree grammatically with this line would leave a sighted reader with fragments.

components.detail.drawnBy.bundle.description: The second rendering: the shipped app, in a device frame. Like components.detail.drawnBy.site it has to stand alone, because the line naming what it answers is read aloud and never drawn.

components.detail.drawnBy.site.description: The first rendering: the component mounted in the workbench’s own React tree. “This site” is the workbench, as against the app. It is read under components.detail.drawnBy, which is not drawn, so it has to be a phrase that stands alone.

components.detail.frameHolds.description: Says which build the device frame is showing. {build} is components.detail.frameHolds.dev or .dist, and <strong> draws it in bold. The tag and the hole have different names because react-intl resolves both out of one map.

components.detail.frameHolds.dev.defaultMessage: the dev server through the proxy
components.detail.frameHolds.dev.description: The {build} of components.detail.frameHolds on a development server. Lower case, because it is dropped into the middle of that sentence.

components.detail.frameHolds.dist.description: The {build} of components.detail.frameHolds in the published build. Lower case, because it is dropped into the middle of that sentence.

components.detail.frameTitle.description: The accessible name of the iframe holding the app. {name} is the component’s name in the source, such as SectionCard, and is not translated.

components.detail.full.description: The button under that line, which gives the frame the whole window.

components.detail.gallery.description: A link into /preview. It says the gallery and not this component on purpose: the preview cannot carry a query on the app’s route, so the frame opens the whole gallery, and the label is what the link does.

components.detail.inherits.defaultMessage: Plus everything in {types}. This repository does not own those, so they are named here and not listed.
components.detail.inherits.description: Printed under the props of a component whose props type extends one from a library. {types} is the list of those type names, drawn in monospace and separated by commas, and is not translated.

components.detail.notDrawn.defaultMessage: Not drawn here: {reason} The bundle draws it.
components.detail.notDrawn.description: Printed under the switch when the first rendering is unavailable. {reason} is a sentence, already ending in a full stop, recorded for this component in components/direct-ids.ts, or components.detail.notDrawn.reason when none is.

components.detail.notDrawn.reason.defaultMessage: the app’s catalogue has no specimen for it.
components.detail.notDrawn.reason.description: The {reason} in components.detail.notDrawn when nothing more specific is recorded. Lower case and ending in a full stop, because it is dropped into the middle of that sentence.

components.detail.prop.noProse.description: Stands in where a prop carries no doc comment. components.card.noDoc says the same about a whole component and reads differently on purpose: that one is about the component’s own comment.

components.detail.prop.optional.description: Appended after a prop’s type, behind a middle dot, for a prop that may be left out. The dot is drawn beside it and is not part of this string.

components.detail.props.none.description: Where the list of props would be, for a component that takes none.

components.detail.reload.description: Both the reload button’s accessible name and its tooltip, on a single component’s page, where the frame holds the app’s gallery. frame.reload is the same words on the preview’s own bar, where the frame holds a whole route.

components.detail.size.auto.defaultMessage: The box this page gives it, whatever that is.
components.detail.size.auto.description: Under the device select when no device is chosen: the drawing simply takes the room the page has.

components.detail.size.column.defaultMessage: Column capped at {width} px. The height is the component’s own.
components.detail.size.column.description: Under the device select while this site is drawing. {width} is the chosen device’s width in CSS pixels; there is no height, because a component drawn here is as tall as its content.

components.detail.size.frame.description: Under the device select while the app’s bundle is drawing. {width} and {height} are the device’s size in CSS pixels and {percent} is how much the frame had to be scaled down to fit.

components.detail.tooNarrow.defaultMessage: The app draws this in a device frame, and the frame needs more width than there is here.
components.detail.tooNarrow.description: Shown in place of the drawing whenever the app’s bundle is what would draw it and the window is too narrow for a device frame: for a component this site cannot draw at all, and for one where the reader has asked for the bundle. The button under it is components.detail.full.

components.detail.twoRenderings.defaultMessage: Two renderings of one component. If they differ, that is a finding, not a flaw. On purpose, nothing compares them automatically.

components.drawn.all.description: The first of the two choices beside the filter: every component, drawn here or not. strings.only.all is the same word on /strings, where it means every string rather than only the ones sharing an English or missing a wording.

components.drawn.here.description: The second of the two choices: only the components this site can draw in its own React tree. “Here” is this page, as against the app’s bundle in a device frame.

components.drawn.legend.description: Read aloud as the group name of the two-way switch beside the filter, and never drawn.

components.empty.description: Where the grid would be, when the filter above the page matches no folder, component or prop. shell.search.empty is the same sentence in the search palette and reads the same in English.

components.filter.description: The accessible name of the filter box in the bar above the page. The bar carries no labels above its fields.

components.filter.placeholder.defaultMessage: Filter, for example Typo, onPress or reader
components.filter.placeholder.description: The placeholder in that box. The three examples are a component, a prop and a folder, one of each; a translation keeps them as they are, because they are identifiers in this repository and not words.

components.filter.summary.description: The count beside the filter box, which follows what is typed into it. {folders} is how many folders still match, {components} how many components, and {drawn} how many of those this site draws in its own React tree rather than in the app’s bundle.

components.lede.defaultMessage: Every component the app builds its screens from, taken out of {root} with its props, their types and whatever prose the source carries.
components.lede.description: The sentence under the heading, which says what the page is. {root} is the directory the components are read out of, drawn in monospace, and is a path rather than a word. The rest of what used to be this paragraph is components.lede.more, behind the ⓘ at its end.

components.lede.more.defaultMessage: Each card draws its component from the app’s source, inside this site. If a card is too small for the whole component, it says so at its lower edge. The component’s own page shows every specimen in full, the app’s own rendering beside it, and a device size. The core’s exports have their own section: <reference>Reference</reference>.
components.lede.more.description: Behind the ⓘ at the end of the sentence under the heading. <reference> is the link to /reference and the word inside it is that page’s own name.

components.modules.defaultMessage: The home screen’s blocks are not here. They belong to one screen and are not components of the app. You find each of them, with its settings, in <editor>the home editor</editor> beside the running app.
components.modules.description: A third paragraph under the lede, saying where the home screen’s blocks are, because they are deliberately not in the grid below. <editor> is the link to the home editor in /preview and the words inside it name that tool.

components.prose.defaultMessage: The sentence under each name is the component’s doc comment from the app’s source. It stays in English, because comments are written for the people who read the code.
components.prose.description: Behind the ⓘ at the end of the sentence under the heading, after components.lede.more. It exists because a German reader meets English prose on every card and is otherwise not told why. Nothing on this page can translate it — it is a JSDoc comment in apps/mobile, and this site prints it as it is written.

components.title.description: The page’s heading. components.detail.crumb is the same word as the first step of the breadcrumb on a single component’s page, which links back here; nav.components is the longer name the rail and the browser tab carry.

conditions.audience.freeMembers.description: Members of the 0 € tier. Inside the app that is somebody whose local newsletter includes it.

conditions.audience.payingMembers.description: Members who pay a contribution, including a trial month and Soli. The door into the app uses the same words.

conditions.byDefault.description: An option in the “Show to” list: the audience the block’s own module chooses when the document says nothing. {audience} is that audience’s name, already translated.

conditions.changeFor.description: The label of the control that says who the change made to a block at this point of the day applies to.

conditions.chip.hasFactChecks.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.hasFactChecks, which is behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.chip.hasLeadArticle.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.hasLeadArticle, which is behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.chip.hasMoreResearch.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.hasMoreResearch, which is behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.chip.hasOpenCallout.defaultMessage: Only while a callout is open
conditions.chip.hasOpenCallout.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.hasOpenCallout, which is behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.chip.hasSpotlightIssue.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.hasSpotlightIssue, which is behind the ⓘ beside it. Spotlight is a newsletter’s name and stays as written.

conditions.chip.loadingOrOffline.description: A small chip in a block’s popover. Short for conditions.intrinsic.loadingOrOffline, which is behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.intrinsic.hasFactChecks.defaultMessage: Appears only when fact checks have loaded.

conditions.intrinsic.hasLeadArticle.defaultMessage: Appears only when there is a lead article: a pinned one or the newest.

conditions.intrinsic.hasMoreResearch.defaultMessage: Appears only when there are more investigations than the lead article.

conditions.intrinsic.hasOpenCallout.defaultMessage: Appears only while a callout is open.
conditions.intrinsic.hasOpenCallout.description: A callout is an open call to readers to send something in; the app calls that screen “Mitmachen”.

conditions.intrinsic.hasSpotlightIssue.defaultMessage: Appears only once a Spotlight issue has loaded.
conditions.intrinsic.hasSpotlightIssue.description: Spotlight is the name of a CORRECTIV newsletter and stays as it is written.

conditions.intrinsic.loadingOrOffline.defaultMessage: Appears only while the app is loading or offline.

conditions.locked.defaultMessage: This change is for another audience. To edit it, sign in a reader from that audience in the frame.
conditions.locked.description: In a block’s popover, where the only change about the block at this point of the day is for an audience the reader signed in in the framed app is not in, so the controls are switched off.

conditions.notFor.defaultMessage: Hidden in the frame. The reader signed in there is not in this audience.
conditions.notFor.description: Under a block that the reader the framed app is signed in as is not in the audience of, which is why the frame does not draw it.

conditions.notYet.defaultMessage: Not yet members (the app is for members only)
conditions.notYet.description: A switched-off option in the “Show to” list. The app admits members only, so no reader of it is not yet a member; whether that changes is an open product question.

conditions.placeFor.description: The label of the control that says who a block is for, all day.

conditions.stranding.defaultMessage: Some audiences cannot be chosen here.
conditions.stranding.description: Under the “This change applies to” list, while some of its options are switched off. Why is conditions.strandingWhy, behind the ⓘ beside it.

conditions.strandingWhy.defaultMessage: This change moves the block away from its other place. If it applied to only some readers, the others would see the block in neither place.
conditions.strandingWhy.description: Behind the ⓘ beside conditions.stranding. The change belongs to a swap of two places at the same time; making it apply to only some readers would leave the others, and readers of older app versions, with neither place.

coreAndHost.adapter.defaultMessage: <muted>adapter </muted><file>lib/platform/expo.ts</file><muted> and </muted><file>lib/audio/backend.ts</file><muted>, the whole cost of adding a host</muted>
coreAndHost.adapter.description: The band across the top of the host’s box, centred. <file> marks a repository path in monospace, which stays as it is written; <muted> is the quieter type around the two paths.

coreAndHost.alt.adapter.defaultMessage: apps/mobile/src/lib/platform/expo.ts answers four of them: the two storage interfaces, the content bundle and the reporter. apps/mobile/src/lib/audio/backend.ts answers the audio one, and apps/mobile/src/app/_layout.tsx composes it onto the other four, so that reasoning about where state is stored does not drag in an audio SDK. Those two files are the whole cost of adding a host.
coreAndHost.alt.adapter.description: What that term says. <code> marks a repository path, which stays as it is written.

coreAndHost.alt.adapter.term.description: The third term in the list under the drawing.

coreAndHost.alt.audio.defaultMessage: AudioBackend: the core needs playback, as status ticks. This host answers with expo-audio’s status events.
coreAndHost.alt.audio.description: One port in that list. <code> marks the interface name, which stays.

coreAndHost.alt.blob.defaultMessage: BlobStore: the core needs the HTTP cache, asynchronously. This host answers with a second MMKV store, which the core’s cache bounds and evicts from. Two stores rather than one is what makes eviction unable to reach a bookmark.
coreAndHost.alt.blob.description: One port in that list. <code> marks the interface name, which stays.

coreAndHost.alt.bundle.defaultMessage: ContentBundle: the core needs what shipped inside the app. This host answers with generated TS modules.
coreAndHost.alt.bundle.description: One port in that list. <code> marks the interface name, which stays.

coreAndHost.alt.core.defaultMessage: Holds stores, articles, media, services, data, lib, ports and types. It imports no UI framework and no platform SDK. packages/app-core/test/boundary.test.ts fails the build on an import matching its list.
coreAndHost.alt.core.description: What that term says. The eight names are the directories of the package and stay as they are written; <code> marks the path of the test.

coreAndHost.alt.core.term.description: The first term in the list under the drawing. <code> marks the package path, which stays as it is written.

coreAndHost.alt.error.defaultMessage: ErrorReporter: the core needs to be heard, for a fault no screen shows. This host answers with one log line, and no provider is chosen yet. It is the one the core does not need in order to work, which is why its default reports nowhere and why the call returns nothing for anyone to wait on. The host’s own error boundary reports through the same implementation, but it reaches it directly rather than across this line.
coreAndHost.alt.error.description: One port in that list. <code> marks the interface name, which stays.

coreAndHost.alt.host.defaultMessage: Expo / React Native, targeting iOS, Android and web.
coreAndHost.alt.host.description: What that term says. The framework and platform names stay as they are written.

coreAndHost.alt.host.term.description: The last term in that list. <code> marks the package path, which stays as it is written.

coreAndHost.alt.keyValue.defaultMessage: KeyValueStore: the core needs small settings, asynchronously. This host answers with MMKV, in the store that holds what the reader chose.
coreAndHost.alt.keyValue.description: One port in that list. <code> marks the interface name, which stays.

coreAndHost.alt.ports.term.defaultMessage: Five ports, the only crossing between the two
coreAndHost.alt.ports.term.description: The second term in that list. The count is read out of this file by test/diagrams.test.ts and held to what CorePlatform declares, so it is load-bearing in English.

coreAndHost.alt.storage.defaultMessage: Both storage ports are asynchronous. What separates them is what they hold, a settings string against a megabyte of cached feeds.
coreAndHost.alt.storage.description: The sentence closing that list of ports.

coreAndHost.answers.description: The heading of the lower half of every one of the five port cards, drawn once per card. coreAndHost.needs is the heading of the upper half.

coreAndHost.asynchronously.description: The second line of what the core needs, on the first two cards. One id because both cards say the word for the same reason: the interface returns a promise.

coreAndHost.audio.answer.1.description: First of two lines of what this host answers AudioBackend with; coreAndHost.audio.answer.2 is the second. expo-audio is the package name and stays.

coreAndHost.audio.answer.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.audio.answer.1.

coreAndHost.audio.needs.1.description: First of two lines of what the core needs of AudioBackend; coreAndHost.audio.needs.2 is the second.

coreAndHost.audio.needs.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.audio.needs.1: the backend reports by handing the core a status at intervals rather than by firing events it has to subscribe to.

coreAndHost.blob.answer.1.description: First of two lines of what this host answers BlobStore with; coreAndHost.blob.answer.2 is the second.

coreAndHost.blob.answer.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.blob.answer.1: the core’s cache holds this store to a size and drops the oldest entry when it is over.

coreAndHost.blob.needs.description: First line of what the core needs of BlobStore; coreAndHost.asynchronously is the second.

coreAndHost.bundle.answer.description: What this host answers ContentBundle with, on one line. TS is TypeScript, abbreviated because the card is 172 units wide.

coreAndHost.bundle.needs.1.description: First of two lines of what the core needs of ContentBundle; coreAndHost.bundle.needs.2 is the second.

coreAndHost.bundle.needs.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.bundle.needs.1.

coreAndHost.calls.description: The verb on the four arrows running down from the core into the ports it needs in order to work. coreAndHost.reports is the verb on the fifth arrow.

coreAndHost.caption.defaultMessage: The core declares the five interfaces and calls them, and a test keeps the line from moving. Four of them it needs in order to work. ErrorReporter it needs in order to be heard: its default reports nowhere, nothing waits for the call, and an unconfigured core goes quiet rather than breaking. This host answers four of them in apps/mobile/src/lib/platform/expo.ts and the audio one in apps/mobile/src/lib/audio/backend.ts, which apps/mobile/src/app/_layout.tsx composes onto the other four. Adding a second host means writing those two files again.
coreAndHost.caption.description: The rest of that caption. <code> marks an interface name or a repository path, which stay as they are written. "the five interfaces" is read out of this file by test/diagrams.test.ts and held to what CorePlatform declares, so the number and the noun beside it are load-bearing in English.

coreAndHost.caption.lead.defaultMessage: Everything that behaves lives above the ports; everything that touches a platform lives below them.
coreAndHost.caption.lead.description: The bold opening of the caption under the drawing.

coreAndHost.core.rule.defaultMessage: Imports no UI framework and no platform SDK. That rule is what gives the package its value.
coreAndHost.core.rule.description: The sentence inside the core’s box, under the row of directory chips.

coreAndHost.core.side.description: The right-hand label on the core’s box, opposite the package path. coreAndHost.host.side is the same label on the host’s box below.

coreAndHost.core.test.defaultMessage: <file>packages/app-core/test/boundary.test.ts</file> fails the build if a platform import ever appears.
coreAndHost.core.test.description: The line under that sentence. <file> marks a repository path drawn in monospace, which stays as it is written.

coreAndHost.error.answer.1.description: First of two lines of what this host answers ErrorReporter with; coreAndHost.error.answer.2 is the second.

coreAndHost.error.answer.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.error.answer.1: no reporting service has been picked.

coreAndHost.error.needs.1.description: First of two lines of what the core needs of ErrorReporter; coreAndHost.error.needs.2 is the second. This is the one card whose upper half says what the core needs in order to be heard rather than in order to work.

coreAndHost.error.needs.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.error.needs.1: a fault nothing in the interface tells the reader about.

coreAndHost.host.side.defaultMessage: the host, all of the platform
coreAndHost.host.side.description: The right-hand label on the host’s box, opposite the package path. coreAndHost.core.side is the same label on the core’s box above.

coreAndHost.host.targets.description: The last line in the host’s box, under the framework names. The three platform names stay as they are written.

coreAndHost.implements.description: The one verb on all five arrows running back up from the host into the ports, because the host answers the fifth exactly as it answers the other four.

coreAndHost.keyValue.answer.1.description: First of two lines of what this host answers KeyValueStore with; coreAndHost.keyValue.answer.2 is the second. MMKV is the name of the storage library and stays.

coreAndHost.keyValue.answer.2.description: Second of the two lines that begin at coreAndHost.keyValue.answer.1. Together they read as one phrase.

coreAndHost.keyValue.needs.description: First line of what the core needs of KeyValueStore; coreAndHost.asynchronously is the second. Each line fits a card 172 units wide at 12px, so about 27 characters.

coreAndHost.lede.defaultMessage: All behaviour on one side, all platform code on the other. They meet only at five named ports. The two small files that answer those ports are all it takes to add a host.

coreAndHost.needs.description: The heading of the upper half of every one of the five port cards, drawn once per card. coreAndHost.answers is the heading of the lower half.

coreAndHost.reports.description: The verb on the fifth arrow down, which has one of its own because the port it reaches is not something the core needs in order to work. coreAndHost.calls is the verb on the other four.

coreAndHost.storage.description: The name of the dashed frame around the first two cards, drawn over the frame’s top edge with a halo behind it.

coreAndHost.storage.note.1.description: First of four hand-wrapped lines under the two storage cards; the others are coreAndHost.storage.note.2, .3 and .4. All four are centred between two arrows 194 units apart, so no line may be wider than that.

coreAndHost.storage.note.2.defaultMessage: by what they hold, a settings
coreAndHost.storage.note.2.description: Second of the four lines that begin at coreAndHost.storage.note.1.

coreAndHost.storage.note.3.description: Third of the four lines that begin at coreAndHost.storage.note.1.

coreAndHost.storage.note.4.description: Last of the four lines that begin at coreAndHost.storage.note.1.

coreAndHost.svg.title.defaultMessage: The core and its host: packages/app-core above, apps/mobile below, joined only by five ports
coreAndHost.svg.title.description: The accessible name of the picture, read aloud in place of it. Never drawn on the page. The two package names are paths and stay as they are.

coreAndHost.title.description: The drawing’s name, as the heading of its own page and on the card that opens it.

decisions.board.lede.defaultMessage: One row per record, oldest first. If a record has struck claims, the reason appears under its title, cut to one sentence. Open a row to see the index’s summary, every struck claim with its full reason, and which records struck it or were struck by it. Nothing in the detail is cut short. The tiles above filter this list too.
decisions.board.lede.description: The paragraph under that heading, which says what a row holds.

decisions.board.title.description: The heading over the table of every record. sources.board.title is the same two words over the table on the sources board.

decisions.caption.defaultMessage: Every architecture decision record in adr/, with what has since been struck inside it.
decisions.caption.description: The table’s caption, drawn as a line above it. <code> holds the directory in this repository the records are read out of, which stays in its own spelling.

decisions.careful.lede.defaultMessage: {careful, plural, one {<f>#</f> record} other {<f>#</f> records}} where the record and the repository are not the same story: {withdrawn, plural, one {one whose own status line is struck through} other {# whose own status lines are struck through}}, and {rest, plural, one {one that decided something} other {# that decided something}} the index says is not built, or not checked on every platform. Everything else on this board was carried out.
decisions.careful.lede.description: The line under that heading. {careful} is how many such records there are, {withdrawn} how many of them have a struck status line, and {rest} how many carry a caveat out of the index instead. All three are counted out of adr/. <f> draws the first figure in monospace.

decisions.careful.read.description: The link on such a card out to the record itself, rendered on this site.

decisions.careful.row.description: The link on such a card down to that record’s row in the table, which it also opens. sources.row is the same word on the sources board’s cards.

decisions.careful.title.description: The heading over the cards for records a reader would be wrong to take at face value.

decisions.collapseAll.description: The button that closes every row’s detail at once. sources.collapseAll is the same two words on the sources board.

decisions.column.decision.description: The third column head, over each record’s own title, its caveats and the one line saying why something in it is no longer true.

decisions.column.record.description: The second column head, over each record’s number and the day it was written.

decisions.column.standing.description: The first column head: whether the record still stands, carries a struck claim, or has been withdrawn.

decisions.column.struck.description: The fourth column head, over how many claims are struck in that record and which later records struck them.

decisions.detail.index.description: Introduces the sentence adr/README.md writes about this record, inside the row’s detail. The sentence itself is the repository’s and is printed as it is written.

decisions.detail.noClause.defaultMessage: No reason follows this strike. The record explains it in the text around it.
decisions.detail.noClause.description: Stands under a struck claim that has no clause after it, so that the gap reads as a fact about the record rather than as a parser that failed. The reason is in the paragraph after the strike, or was taken by a second strike beside it.

decisions.detail.read.description: The link out of the row’s detail to the record itself, rendered on this site. {number} is the record’s four-digit number. “ADR” is what this repository calls these documents and is left in its own spelling.

decisions.detail.struck.defaultMessage: {count, plural, one {One claim is struck:} other {# claims are struck:}}
decisions.detail.struck.description: Introduces the list of struck claims inside the row’s detail. {count} is how many claims are struck in this record.

decisions.detail.voids.defaultMessage: {count, plural, one {It struck a claim in} other {It struck claims in}}
decisions.detail.voids.description: Introduces the chips of the records this one struck something in, inside the row’s detail. {count} is how many records those are, and it is not drawn: the chips that follow are the list.

decisions.details.description: The button at the end of a row that opens its detail, and the name of the column those buttons sit in, which is read aloud and never drawn. sources.details is the same word on the sources board.

decisions.expandAll.description: The button that opens every row’s detail at once. sources.expandAll is the same two words on the sources board.

decisions.eyebrow.description: The small line over the page heading, which says what site this is. sources.eyebrow is the same line word for word over the sources board, and the two are separate ids because each page owns its own header.

decisions.filter.description: The label over the text field above the table. sources.filter is the same shape of label over the sources board’s field and reads “Filter rows”.

decisions.filter.placeholder.description: The placeholder in that field, naming the three things the filter reads. It matches a record’s number, its title, its status, the index’s sentence and the text of every struck claim and clause.

decisions.footer.build.defaultMessage: Every row, count and link above is read from the records themselves when the site is built. The workbench keeps no copy, so this board cannot disagree with adr/. If it cannot read a record, the site does not build.
decisions.footer.build.description: The first line of the footer, which says where the board comes from. <code> holds the directory in this repository, which stays in its own spelling.

decisions.footer.label.description: The footer’s one visible line, beside an ⓘ that opens the two paragraphs below. sources.footer.label reads the same in English on the sources board, which is a different board built out of different files.

decisions.footer.notes.defaultMessage: The index these sentences come from is published in full at <notes>Decisions, the notes</notes>. It also has what a table cannot hold: notes for readers of the older records, and the rule above in full.
decisions.footer.notes.description: The second line of the footer. <notes> is the link to /decisions-notes, and the words inside it are this site’s name for that page. The document behind it is adr/README.md and stays English.

decisions.hide.description: What the Details button says while that row’s detail is open. sources.hide is the same word on the sources board.

decisions.lede.defaultMessage: The choices this repository argued rather than assumed, and which of them still hold. A record says why. The architecture says what the thing is.
decisions.lede.description: The paragraph under the heading. <em> emphasises one word and <architecture> is the link to /architecture, which is the repository’s ARCHITECTURE.md rendered on this site.

decisions.only.defaultMessage: Only what is not built or not checked
decisions.only.description: The checkbox beside that field. It keeps the records whose own index entry says the decision was not carried out, or was not verified on every platform.

decisions.reason.struck.description: Read aloud before the one line of reason under the title of a record carrying a struck claim, and never drawn. decisions.reason.withdrawn is the same announcement on a record whose own status line is struck through.

decisions.reason.withdrawn.description: Read aloud before the one line of reason under a withdrawn record’s title, and never drawn. Without it the line is a fragment of a document and a screen reader gets no warning that the row has changed subject. decisions.reason.struck is the same announcement on a record that merely carries a struck claim.

decisions.recordName.description: Read aloud after a control that would otherwise announce as a bare number or as the word Details, and never drawn. {number} is the record’s four-digit number and {title} its own English title out of adr/, which is not translated. The leading comma is a pause: the visible text comes first.

decisions.rule.clauseless.defaultMessage: {count, plural, one {<f>#</f> of them has no reason attached. The reason was in the paragraph after the strike, or a second strike beside it took it, and the board cannot match either automatically. That row says so, and the record itself has the answer.} other {<f>#</f> of them have no reason attached. The reason was in the paragraph after the strike, or a second strike beside it took it, and the board cannot match either automatically. Those rows say so, and the record itself has the answer.}}
decisions.rule.clauseless.description: The fourth paragraph of that note, drawn only while {count} is above zero. {count} is how many struck claims have no clause after them at all, which is a smaller set than the strikes naming no record. <f> draws the figure in monospace.

decisions.rule.label.defaultMessage: How an expired claim is marked
decisions.rule.label.description: The visible label of the ⓘ under the lede, which opens the four paragraphs of the rule and its counts.

decisions.rule.never.defaultMessage: A record is never rewritten to look right later. When a later decision makes a claim false, the claim is struck through where it stands. One short reason says what voided it, with a link to the record that did. The argument around it stays as it was, because the reasoning is what is worth keeping.
decisions.rule.never.description: The first paragraph behind that ⓘ, and this repository’s rule for its own records in one sentence. <strong> carries the rule itself and <em> the one word the rule turns on.

decisions.rule.struck.defaultMessage: So <f>{struck}</f> {struck, plural, one {claim is} other {claims are}} struck across these <f>{records}</f> records, and a record with a struck claim still stands. That is the rule working, not a fault. This board makes it visible. In the documents themselves, you would have to open all {records}.
decisions.rule.struck.description: The second paragraph of that note. {struck} is how many claims are struck through across every record, {records} how many records there are; both are counted out of adr/ at build time. <f> draws a figure in monospace so it is never mistaken for prose.

decisions.rule.unattributed.defaultMessage: {count, plural, one {<f>#</f> of those strikes names no later record. A new measurement or a later section of the same record struck it. So there is no arrow to draw, and its reason is all there is to say.} other {<f>#</f> of those strikes name no later record. A new measurement or a later section of the same record struck them. So there is no arrow to draw, and their reason is all there is to say.}} A row shows that reason under its title, cut to one sentence. The detail below has all of them in full.
decisions.rule.unattributed.description: The third paragraph of that note. {count} is how many struck claims name no record with a higher number, so the board has no edge to draw for them. <f> draws the figure in monospace. Both branches carry the whole first half of the paragraph, because the pronouns after the count change with it.

decisions.show.legend.description: Read aloud as the group name of the four filter tiles, and never drawn: the heading beside it is what a reader sees.

decisions.show.title.description: The heading over the four filter tiles. sources.show.title is the same word over the tiles of the sources board.

decisions.showing.defaultMessage: Showing {shown} of {total, plural, one {# record} other {# records}}
decisions.showing.description: The live count beside the filters. {shown} is how many rows the filters leave and {total} how many records there are altogether.

decisions.standing.partly.description: The chip on a record whose decision holds but which carries at least one struck claim, and the accessible name of the tile that filters for those.

decisions.standing.partly.meaning.defaultMessage: The decision holds. Claims inside it do not, and are struck where they stand rather than rewritten.
decisions.standing.partly.meaning.description: The line under the Partly struck tile, which says what that standing means.

decisions.standing.stands.description: The chip on a record nothing has struck, and the accessible name of the tile that filters for those. It means the record is still true as written.

decisions.standing.stands.meaning.defaultMessage: Nothing in them has been made false since they were written.
decisions.standing.stands.meaning.description: The line under the Stands tile, which says what that standing means.

decisions.standing.withdrawn.description: The chip on a record whose own status line is struck through, and the accessible name of the tile that filters for those. It is the one standing a reader could act on and be wrong.

decisions.standing.withdrawn.meaning.defaultMessage: The status line itself is struck through. Read the record as history.
decisions.standing.withdrawn.meaning.description: The line under the No longer stands tile, which says what that standing means.

decisions.struck.by.description: Introduces the chips of the later records that struck something in this one, in the Struck claims cell. Lower case and mid-sentence: the chips finish the line.

decisions.struck.count.description: The count in the Struck claims cell, drawn only where {count} is above one: a single strike says nothing the standing chip has not already said. <n> draws the figure and <w> the word after it, which is why the two are tagged apart.

decisions.struck.finding.description: Stands where those chips would be, on the commonest case: a strike whose clause names no record, so there is nothing to link to. Deliberately not “by no later record”, which reads as missing data about the majority of the strikes on this board.

decisions.struck.none.description: The Struck claims cell of a record nothing has been struck in. Lower case, because it completes the column head rather than starting a sentence.

decisions.tile.all.description: The first filter tile, which switches the standing filter off. It is also the tile’s accessible name, because the card as a whole is the control.

decisions.tile.all.note.defaultMessage: Written between <f>{from}</f> and <f>{to}</f>, in the order they were taken.
decisions.tile.all.note.description: The line under that tile. {from} is the ISO day of the oldest record and {to} of the newest, both read out of adr/. <f> draws each day in monospace so it never wraps.

decisions.title.description: The page’s heading. nav.decisions is the same two words as the browser tab and the search palette carry for this page; shell.activity.decisions is the shorter word the rail has room for.

decisionsChain.lede.defaultMessage: {records} records, never rewritten. When a later decision makes an earlier claim false, the claim is struck through, and the later record names what it retired. Read a row to see whether a record still holds. Follow the arcs to see which record changed it.
decisionsChain.lede.description: The paragraph under that heading. {records} is how many records adr/ holds, counted by the drawing’s own layout rather than typed. test/diagrams.test.ts holds it to that count, so the placeholder has to stay at the front of the sentence.

decisionsChain.title.defaultMessage: Which decisions still stand, and which of their claims do not
decisionsChain.title.description: The drawing’s name, as the heading of its own page and on the card that opens it.

design.board.description: The second of the three cards. The board is the inventory of screens the plugin draws into the Figma file.

design.board.note.defaultMessage: {path} draws the overview of all screens into the file, from data in this repository. Nobody has to keep a board up to date by hand.
design.board.note.description: The line in the board card. {path} is the plugin’s directory in this repository and is not translated; <code> draws it in monospace.

design.clients.fork.description: Under the Linux download. figma-linux-next is the project’s own name and is not translated; the rest says what it is, because Figma builds no client for Linux.

design.clients.note.defaultMessage: You load the plugin through Plugins, Development, Import plugin from manifest. That menu exists only in the desktop app. Figma makes one for macOS and Windows; on Linux this project uses a fork.
design.clients.note.description: The line above the four downloads. “Plugins, Development, Import plugin from manifest” is Figma’s own menu and stays in English in every catalogue: it is not a description of a menu, it is the words a reader has to find in one. macOS, Windows and Linux are the platforms’ own names.

design.clients.official.description: Under each of the three downloads Figma itself builds, as against the Linux fork under design.clients.fork.

design.colours.description: The first of the three cards saying where the design reaches the code. This one is about the shared palette.

design.colours.note.defaultMessage: Not copied from the file. {pkg} is generated, and the app and this site import the same stylesheet. So {token} means the same thing in three places.
design.colours.note.description: The line in the colours card. {pkg} is the design-tokens package and {token} one of its classes; both are identifiers and are not translated. <code> draws each in monospace.

design.frameTitle.description: The accessible name of the frame that holds the design file, read aloud and never drawn. {file} is the Figma file’s own name and is not translated.

design.full.description: The button on the narrow layout, where the frame does not fit beside the page. It opens the view full screen and loads nothing; design.load is the button that fetches the file. components.detail.full is the same words on a component’s page, where what opens full screen is the app.

design.full.note.defaultMessage: The frame needs the full width of the screen, so it opens on its own. The file still loads only when you press the button.
design.full.note.description: The line under the full-screen button. design.load.note is the line under the other button, which does fetch the file.

design.lede.defaultMessage: The app is designed in one Figma file, {file}. It is the source for the screens, and this workbench is the source for everything written down about them.
design.lede.description: The paragraph under the heading. {file} is the Figma file’s own name and is not translated; <b> draws it in bold.

design.links.app.description: The second card in the Open tool, which goes to /preview.

design.links.file.description: The first card in the Open tool, which leaves for the design file itself. design.open is the same door as a button in the bar above the page.

design.links.note.defaultMessage: The preview shows the running app at the size the file draws it, so you can compare the two.

design.load.description: The button that makes the one request to figma.com. Nothing is fetched until it is pressed, which is why the box above it says what will be.

design.load.note.description: The line under the load button, naming the third party the request goes to. design.full.note is the line under the other button, which fetches nothing.

design.loads.description: The first heading in the box above the button, over the address a press will fetch. The address itself is printed in monospace and is not a message.

design.loads.note.defaultMessage: One request to figma.com, and none before the button is pressed.

design.open.description: The button in the bar above the page that leaves this site for the file in Figma itself. design.links.file is the same door in the tool panel, worded as a place rather than as an action.

design.plugin.description: The third of the three cards, about the program that draws the board.

design.plugin.doc.description: The link to the plugin’s own documentation, which is that README rendered as a page of this site. It reads the same as the document’s name in the repository’s registry, which is not a message.

design.plugin.note.defaultMessage: {codeFile} knows nothing about the app. It draws whatever {specFile} describes. Its documentation is a page on this site and covers the traps of the Linux client.
design.plugin.note.description: The line in the plugin card. {codeFile} and {specFile} are two file names in the plugin’s directory and are not translated; <code> draws each in monospace.

design.plugin.repo.description: The link beside it, which leaves this site for the plugin’s directory on GitHub at the commit this page was built from.

design.reload.description: Both the reload button’s accessible name and its tooltip, on this page, where the frame holds the Figma file. frame.reload is the same words on the preview’s bar, where the frame holds a whole route of the app, and components.detail.reload on a component’s page, where it holds the gallery.

design.rest.below.defaultMessage: More about the design is below: the desktop apps, the plugin, and where the colours reach the code.
design.rest.below.description: Where the three tools are, on a layout too narrow for the right-hand panel. design.rest.side is the same sentence for the wide layout.

design.rest.side.defaultMessage: More about the design is on the right: the desktop apps, the plugin, and where the colours reach the code.
design.rest.side.description: Where the three tools are, on a layout wide enough to put them in the right-hand panel. design.rest.below is the same sentence for the layout that stacks them under the page.

design.see.description: The second heading in that box, over what the frame will show once it loads.

design.see.note.defaultMessage: The file, if you are signed in to Figma and have access. Otherwise Figma’s sign-in page. That is a question of access, not an error: the file is not shared publicly.

design.title.description: The heading over the page that frames the Figma file. shell.activity.design is the same word on the rail, landing.door.design.title on the front page’s card, and nav.design is the longer name the browser tab carries.

devices.breakpoint.description: Not a device: the width the reader’s own stylesheet changes at, worth being able to sit exactly on. 48rem is a CSS length and stays as it is written.

devices.custom.description: The last entry in the device picker: a width and a height the reader types, or drags the stage handles to. Choosing it is what makes the two number fields on the bar appear.

devices.desktop.description: A size, not a model: a window the size a desktop screen opens one at. devices.laptop is the smaller of the same pair.

devices.host.description: The first entry in the device picker: no device frame at all, the app drawn at whatever size the page has. It states a size rather than naming one, because this is the one entry with no number beside it.

devices.laptop.description: A size, not a model: a window the size a laptop opens one at. devices.desktop is the larger of the same pair.

diagrams.breadcrumb.description: Read aloud as the name of the trail above the drawing, and never drawn. The trail itself is the handbook, the drawings, and where this one is in the set.

diagrams.crumb.description: The second step of that trail, which is the name of the page it links to. diagrams.title is that page’s own heading and handbook.card.diagrams is the card that opens it; all three read the same in English and are three entries because one is a heading, one is a card and one is a link in a trail.

diagrams.figure.alt.defaultMessage: The same diagram as a list
diagrams.figure.alt.description: The heading over the list beneath a drawing. That list is not a caption: it is the page for anyone who cannot use the picture.

diagrams.figure.scroll.description: The name of the box a drawing scrolls sideways inside, read aloud and never drawn. {number} is the drawing’s place in the set, counted from one, and is the same number the page shows in its breadcrumb.

diagrams.lede.defaultMessage: The architecture the handbook describes, as drawings.
diagrams.lede.description: The sentence under the heading, which says what the page is. The rest of what used to be this paragraph is diagrams.lede.more, behind the ⓘ at its end.

diagrams.lede.more.defaultMessage: Each drawing is hand-written SVG and takes all of its colours from classes. So it follows the light and dark scheme by itself, and there is no second file to keep in step.
diagrams.lede.more.description: Behind the ⓘ at the end of the sentence under the heading, followed there by diagrams.list.

diagrams.list.defaultMessage: Under every drawing, the same content appears as a list. The list is not a caption. It is the page for anyone who cannot use the picture.

diagrams.others.description: Read aloud as the name of the navigation at the foot of the page, which holds the drawing before this one and the one after it, and is never drawn.

diagrams.position.description: The last step of the trail, which says where this drawing is in the set rather than naming it: the drawing’s own title is the heading directly underneath. {position} is its number from one and {total} is how many drawings there are.

diagrams.title.description: The page’s heading. handbook.card.diagrams is the card on /handbook that opens this page and diagrams.crumb is the step in a single drawing’s breadcrumb that leads back to it; all three read the same in English. nav.diagrams is the longer name the browser tab carries.

document.breadcrumb.description: Read aloud as the name of the trail above a document, and never drawn. The trail itself is the section the rail lights and then the document’s own name, both of which come out of the repository. components.detail.breadcrumb is the same word over a single component’s page.

document.neighbours.defaultMessage: The records either side of this one
document.neighbours.description: Read aloud as the name of the two cards at the foot of a record, and never drawn. Records are a chain, and reading two in a row is the ordinary way to use them.

document.next.description: The kicker on the right-hand card at the foot of a record. {nav} is the neighbouring record’s own short name out of the repository and is not translated. document.previous is the card on the other side.

document.previous.description: The kicker on the left-hand card at the foot of a record. {nav} is the neighbouring record’s own short name out of the repository and is not translated. document.next is the card on the other side.

document.retired.badge.description: The badge at the head of a document that has struck claims in it. {count} is how many, and is never zero because the badge is not drawn then. English does not inflect the word; the plural is here so that a language which does has somewhere to say so.

document.retired.note.defaultMessage: {count, plural, one {One claim on this page is struck through.} other {Some claims on this page are struck through.}} The reason stands beside each.
document.retired.note.description: The sentence beside that badge, saying what the strikes on the page mean. {count} is how many claims are struck, and decides only whether the sentence is singular.

document.retired.tag.description: The chip drawn on each struck claim, against the clause that says what voided it. One word, in small type, inside the annotation rather than in the document: it is this site’s label and not the record’s text.

document.source.defaultMessage: This page is <fileLink>{file}</fileLink> in the repository, shown here. It is not a copy, so there is only one place to edit it.
document.source.description: The line at the foot of a document read out of the repository. {file} is its path and is not translated; <fileLink> is the link to it on GitHub at the commit this site was built from. document.source.generated is the same line for the one document that is written by a program.

document.source.generated.defaultMessage: A program writes this page: <fileLink>{file}</fileLink> in the repository. It runs when the site is built, so there is nothing here to edit.
document.source.generated.description: The line at the foot of the one document that is generated rather than read. {file} is the path of the PROGRAM and is not translated; <fileLink> is the link to it. document.source offers every other document as a file to edit, and offering this one would be an invitation to type into an output.

drawing.failed.description: Stands where a component of the app should have been drawn, on a surface of this site, after that component threw. {message} is the error’s own message out of the app’s source and is not translated.

edition.band.description: Read out for the coloured band an edition draws along the track. {edition} is the edition’s own title as the newsroom wrote it, or its id where it has none; {from} and {to} are times of day, as 18:00, and {to} is 24:00 where the edition runs on past midnight.

edition.days.description: The accessible name of an edition’s band in the week or month under the frame. {edition} is its title as the newsroom wrote it, or its id. {sameMonth} is yes when its first and last day are in one month, and then {month} is that month’s name and {fromDay} and {toDay} the two days’ numbers; otherwise {from} and {to} are the two days in full, as “September 27”.

edition.decides.description: Read out for the coloured hairline at a block’s edge, which marks a block whose state at the playhead an edition sets rather than the ordinary day. {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id where it has none.

edition.details.description: The accessible name of the button that opens the edition’s popover, and of the popover itself. {edition} is its title, or its id where it has none.

edition.end.description: Stands where a time would inside edition.start and edition.momentSpan, when nothing else happens before the edition is over. Lower case, mid-sentence.

edition.from.description: The label of the field for the date and time the edition starts. Every time in the home document is Berlin wall-clock time, whatever the browser’s own zone is, which is why the label says so.

edition.here.description: The visible word on the button beside the track that starts an edition at the playhead. An edition is a named layer over the ordinary day, a campaign or an election night, active for a span of dates. edition.hereLong is the same button’s accessible name.

edition.hereLong.defaultMessage: Start a one-day edition at this minute
edition.hereLong.description: The accessible name of the button whose visible word is edition.here. The new edition starts at the playhead and ends at the same minute the next day; its popover in the panel changes both.

edition.kind.description: The small word before an edition’s name at the head of the panel. An edition is a named layer over the ordinary day, a campaign or an election night, active from one date and time until another.

edition.landsOn.defaultMessage: Your changes go into the edition “{edition}”.
edition.landsOn.description: Says which layer an edit in the panel writes to while an edition is running at the playhead: the narrowest one, which is the one whose word the phone shows. {edition} is its title as the newsroom wrote it, or its id where it has none.

edition.landsOnDay.defaultMessage: Your changes go into the ordinary day.
edition.landsOnDay.description: Says which layer of the home document an edit in the panel writes to, when no edition is running at the playhead. edition.landsOn is the same line while one is.

edition.momentGo.description: The accessible name of a stop an edition draws on the track, for one of its own moments. {time} is a time of day, as 23:00; {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id where it has none.

edition.momentRemove.description: The accessible name of the button that deletes the edition’s moment being edited. {time} is its time of day, as 23:00; {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id where it has none.

edition.momentSpan.defaultMessage: until {until} · {changes, plural, =0 {nothing changes here yet} other {# changed here}}
edition.momentSpan.description: Beside the time field of a moment of an edition: how long it lasts and how much it changes. {until} is when the edition’s next moment takes over, as 23:00, or edition.end; {changes} is how many blocks it differs on. home.point.span is the same sentence for a moment of the day.

edition.momentTime.defaultMessage: The time of this moment of the edition
edition.momentTime.description: The label of the time field for a moment of an edition. Read aloud, not drawn.

edition.offIn.description: Says when a switched-off block is off, in its details popover, while an edition’s starting state is being edited. {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id.

edition.oneDay.description: The accessible name of an edition’s band in the week or month under the frame, for an edition on one day only. {edition} is its title, or its id; {day} is the day, as “27 September”.

edition.pinEarly.defaultMessage: This pin is public as soon as the edition is. To lead with an embargoed piece, use its flag in WordPress instead.
edition.pinEarly.description: Shown beside a pinned article inside an edition, and in the edition’s popover when it pins one. The flag is the WordPress field that makes an article lead the app, which is set at publication and so never earlier than the article itself.

edition.publicWhenMerged.defaultMessage: An edition is public as soon as it is merged. Submit it only once it may be known.
edition.publicWhenMerged.description: A warning in the edition’s popover. The repository is public, and the private plan that would keep a dated edition out of it until shortly before it starts is not built yet, so this is the whole of the protection for now.

edition.remove.description: Takes the whole edition out of the document, with everything it changes. The ordinary day is untouched by it.

edition.start.description: Names the point being edited when it is the edition’s own starting state rather than one of its moments. {until} is when its first moment takes over, as 23:00, or edition.end where none does.

edition.switchOffIn.description: The same button on a block that is on. {block} is the block’s own name; {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id.

edition.switchOnIn.description: The accessible name of the eye button on a block that is off, while an edition’s starting state is what an edit writes to. {block} is the block’s own name; {edition} is the edition’s title, or its id.

edition.taken.defaultMessage: An edition already starts at exactly this minute. Edit that one instead.
edition.taken.description: The tooltip on edition.here when it is switched off: a new edition here could not be narrower than the one already running, so it would never be the one an edit lands on.

edition.title.description: The label of the field for the newsroom’s own name for the edition, which is data in the document and never translated. Empty means none, and the id stands in for it.

edition.until.description: The label of the field for the date and time the edition ends. At that minute it is already over, which “ends at” says without a note. An end at or before the start is not taken, and the field springs back.

fixtures.bigType.hint.defaultMessage: A++ (1.15), chosen in the app: it replaces the system text size on every screen, the article included.
fixtures.bigType.hint.description: The line under the “Largest text scale” fixture. A++ is the app’s own name for that step of the text-size control and stays as it is written; 1.15 is the size the whole app is drawn at, in place of the device’s own text size rather than on top of it.

fixtures.bundle.description: A fixture in the state tool: the app falls back to the articles shipped inside the binary, because nothing fresher is in the cache.

fixtures.bundle.hint.defaultMessage: The app shows only the content it shipped with, as if offline.
fixtures.bundle.hint.description: The line under the “Bundled content only” fixture. “offline” is the literal value of the feed status in the core’s own state and stays as it is written.

fixtures.freeMember.description: A fixture in the state tool: a member of the 0 € tier whose local newsletter subscription includes the app.

fixtures.freeMember.hint.defaultMessage: A free member instead of a paying one. The app starts on Home.
fixtures.freeMember.hint.description: The line under the “Free member, local newsletter” fixture. “Home” is the app’s first tab, which the app itself calls “Start”.

fixtures.fresh.hint.defaultMessage: Nothing stored. The app starts at the sign-in, signed out.
fixtures.fresh.hint.description: The line under the “Fresh install” fixture. “The door” is the sign-in gate the app’s root layout renders in place of every route until a session carries an entitlement; every hint in this group calls it that.

fixtures.interests.hint.defaultMessage: A personal Home: more feeds, and blocks in a different order.
fixtures.interests.hint.description: The line under the “Interests picked” fixture. “Home” is the app’s first tab, which the app itself calls “Start”; a module is one block of that screen.

fixtures.noAccess.hint.defaultMessage: A member paying 0 €. The sign-in sends them to the upgrade.
fixtures.noAccess.hint.description: The line under the “Signed in, no app access” fixture. The 0 € tier is CORRECTIV’s free membership, which does not include the app; 0 € is a price and stays as it is written.

fixtures.onboarded.hint.defaultMessage: The ordinary case: the app starts on Home.
fixtures.onboarded.hint.description: The line under the “Onboarded” fixture. “Home” is the app’s first tab, which the app itself calls “Start”.

fixtures.saved.hint.defaultMessage: Without this, the Saved tab is empty.
fixtures.saved.hint.description: The line under the “Saved articles” fixture. /gespeichert is a route in the app and stays in its own spelling.

fixtures.signedIn.hint.defaultMessage: A member’s first start: past the sign-in, into the onboarding.

fixtures.submitted.description: A fixture in the state tool. A callout is an open call to readers to send something in; the app calls that screen “Mitmachen”.

fixtures.submitted.hint.defaultMessage: The form shows its thank-you instead of the questions.

frame.copied.description: Announced in a live region for a second and a half after the address has been copied. Read aloud and never seen.

frame.copyLink.defaultMessage: Copy this view as a link
frame.copyLink.description: Both the copy button’s accessible name and its tooltip.

frame.day.hideTip.defaultMessage: The day · press to put it away

frame.day.show.defaultMessage: Show the day under the frame
frame.day.show.description: Says what pressing does while the timeline is away, and is both the button’s accessible name and its tooltip.

frame.device.description: The accessible name of the select that picks which device the app is framed at. The bar carries no labels above its fields.

frame.language.description: The accessible name of the select that chooses which language the framed app runs in. This is the APP’s language, not this site’s, which is in the settings dialog. The bar carries no labels above its fields.

frame.language.shipped.description: The one option of the app-language select that is a word rather than a locale code: leave the app in the language it ships, which is what an address naming no language asks for.

frame.more.defaultMessage: More frame controls: language, zoom, reload, open without the frame
frame.more.description: The accessible name of the button that unfolds the controls that do not fit below 640px.

frame.more.tip.defaultMessage: Language, zoom, reload, open without the frame

frame.orientation.landscape.description: One of the two segments of the orientation control. A term of art.

frame.orientation.landscapeTip.description: The tooltip on the one-icon orientation toggle below 640px, saying which way the frame is up now.

frame.orientation.legend.description: The legend of the two-segment orientation control at 640px and up. Read aloud and not drawn.

frame.orientation.portrait.description: One of the two segments of the orientation control. A term of art.

frame.orientation.portraitTip.description: The tooltip on the one-icon orientation toggle below 640px, saying which way the frame is up now.

frame.pages.empty.defaultMessage: No page by that name. You can type any address into the field beside this.
frame.pages.empty.description: Stands in for the list when the typed filter matches nothing. The field it points at is the route field to the right of this button.

frame.pages.gallery.description: The app’s own gallery screen, which this site named because the screen is a development surface with no name in the product.

frame.pages.gallery.note.defaultMessage: every component, twice, on both surfaces

frame.pages.gespeichert.description: Beside the saved-articles screen. A FlatList is React Native’s own name for the component, and is not translated.

frame.pages.group.screens.description: The group of the app’s screens that are not tabs and take no id.

frame.pages.group.tabs.description: The group of the app’s five tab-bar screens, in the page picker.

frame.pages.group.withAnId.description: The group of route shapes whose last segment names one article, project or claim. The address in each row is one example of the shape.

frame.pages.group.worthReaching.description: The group of two addresses that are not screens of the app in the ordinary sense: its component gallery and its 404.

frame.pages.home.description: The app’s first tab. One of the three entries in the picker this site had to name itself, because the screen carries no name of its own the way Entdecken and Mediathek do.

frame.pages.notFound.description: The app’s own 404 screen, in the picker. nav.title.notFound is this SITE’s 404 in the browser tab and reads the same in English.

frame.pages.notFound.note.defaultMessage: any address the app has no route for

frame.pages.open.description: Four things at once, all the same words: the button’s accessible name, its tooltip, the dialog’s own name and the placeholder in the field that filters the list.

frame.pages.player.defaultMessage: a modal over the running audio

frame.pages.serie.description: Beside the podcast series screen. A FlatList is React Native’s own name for the component, and is not translated; the first one is frame.pages.gespeichert.

frame.raw.defaultMessage: Open the app on its own, without the frame
frame.raw.description: The accessible name of the button that leaves this site for the app itself. frame.raw.tip is the shorter tooltip beside it.

frame.raw.devTip.defaultMessage: Open the app without the frame · a dev server applies no base path, so this lands on the app’s 404

frame.raw.tip.defaultMessage: Open the app without the frame

frame.reload.description: Both the reload button’s accessible name and its tooltip, on the preview’s own bar. The frame there holds a whole route of the app. components.detail.reload is the same words on a single component’s page, where the frame holds the gallery.

frame.route.description: The accessible name of the field the app’s address is typed into.

frame.stage.heading.description: The heading of the area the app is drawn in, read aloud and never seen. frame.stage.title is the frame element’s own name one level in.

frame.stage.title.description: The name of the iframe the app runs in, which is what a screen reader says before it steps into it. frame.stage.heading is the heading above it.

frame.toolbar.description: The accessible name of the whole control bar above the framed app. Read aloud and never seen.

frame.zoom.description: The accessible name of the select that scales the frame.

frame.zoom.fit.description: The one option of the zoom select that is a word rather than a percentage: scale the frame to whatever room the stage has.

handbook.card.architecture.kind.description: The kicker over the Architecture card: what kind of document it is.

handbook.card.conventions.kind.description: The kicker over the Conventions card: what kind of document it is.

handbook.card.diagrams.description: The card that opens the drawings. diagrams.title is the heading of the page it opens and diagrams.crumb is the step in a single drawing’s breadcrumb that leads back to it; all three read the same in English.

handbook.card.diagrams.blurb.defaultMessage: The same architecture, drawn: the core and its host, which decisions still stand, what the app talks to, how the core is layered inside, how somebody signs in, and where an article comes from.
handbook.card.diagrams.blurb.description: The sentence under the Diagrams card, and the only card sentence on this page that is not read out of the repository: there is no Markdown document at that route to have written one.

handbook.card.diagrams.kind.description: The kicker over the Diagrams card. The other kickers on this page name a kind of prose; this one says the section is pictures.

handbook.card.provenance.kind.description: The kicker over the Provenance card. It is the one document on this grid that is written by a program out of the repository rather than read out of it.

handbook.card.readme.kind.description: The kicker over the Readme card: this is the document to arrive at first.

handbook.card.release.kind.description: The kicker over the Release card: the document is a sequence of steps.

handbook.card.traps.kind.description: The kicker over the Traps card. It says how the document was come by rather than what it is: every line in it was paid for by a failure that passed every check.

handbook.lede.defaultMessage: The repository’s own documents, shown straight from their files.
handbook.lede.description: The sentence under the heading, which says what the page is. The rest of what used to be this paragraph is handbook.lede.more, behind the ⓘ at its end.

handbook.lede.more.defaultMessage: Nothing here is a copy. The files are the source, and this site is a second way to read them. So there is one place to edit, and no version quietly falls behind.
handbook.lede.more.description: Behind the ⓘ at the end of the sentence under the heading, followed there by handbook.records.

handbook.records.defaultMessage: The decisions behind all this have their own section. A decision record is a different kind of document: it is never rewritten. When a later decision makes a claim false, the claim is struck through, not corrected.

handbook.title.description: The page’s heading. shell.activity.handbook is the rail entry that opens it and the word a document’s breadcrumb uses for this section; nav.handbook is the same word again as the page’s name in the browser tab and the search palette.

home.block.empty.description: Stands in for a block that measured no height at all, in place of an empty box that would read as a block that is broken. {block} is the module’s own name, which this strip carries because the list around it shows no names.

home.block.name.description: How a block is named to a screen reader, wherever a control has to say which one it means. {name} is the module’s label out of MODULE_LABELS and {id} the section’s own id, which is on screen at the end of every row. A translation keeps the brackets: the id is an identifier and the two halves must stay tellable apart.

home.block.unknown.defaultMessage: Not shown: the app has no block called <name>{module}</name>.
home.block.unknown.description: Stands in for a block whose module this app has no renderer for, which happens while the document is ahead of the app. {module} is the word the document used, drawn in a monospace face.

home.calendar.chosen.description: Read out when several days have been chosen with Shift and an arrow key, or by dragging. {from} and {to} are the first and last day, as “28 September”.

home.calendar.refused.defaultMessage: Editions that take precedence already cover all of these days. Edit one of those instead.
home.calendar.refused.description: Shown under the week or month when a drag across days made no edition: every minute of those days already belongs to a narrower edition, or one runs over exactly those days, so a new one would never be the one an edit lands on.

home.calendar.today.description: The accessible name of the column for today in the week or month under the frame. {day} is the date already spelled by the browser, as “Monday, 28 September”.

home.document.changed.description: The word beside Submit changes while the document differs from the file. home.row.changed is the badge on a single block’s row and tools.tokens.changed the badge on an overridden colour; all three read the same in English.

home.document.field.description: The name read out for the field that holds the issue’s text when the clipboard was refused.

home.document.follow.defaultMessage: Scroll the frame to the block you point at

home.document.refused.description: The badge in front of the dev server’s reason for not writing the file. White on the brand red, beside a sentence that comes from the server and is not translated.

home.document.revert.description: Throws away every edit of this session and goes back to the document as the repository has it.

home.document.rule.defaultMessage: A moment holds only what changes at that time. Everything else carries on as before.
home.document.rule.description: Behind the ⓘ in the head of the point being edited, and the one rule that makes the rest legible: a moment holds the difference from the point before it rather than the whole state.

home.document.saveNote.defaultMessage: On a dev server, Save writes {file} in your own checkout. It refuses anything the core cannot read. This is a shortcut for developers. The way to a pull request is Submit changes.
home.document.saveNote.description: Says what Save does before anybody presses it, on a dev server only. The tag wraps {file}, the repository path of the document, drawn in a monospace face.

home.document.scenarioGuard.defaultMessage: Scenarios are examples. They are not submitted.
home.document.scenarioGuard.description: Under the switched-off Submit changes, and under the switched-off Save on a dev server, while a scenario is open or the document still holds one. Submitting or saving it would publish the example on every phone.

home.document.submit.description: The editor’s primary action, on the published site and on a dev server alike. It opens a prefilled GitHub issue in a new tab, which a workflow turns into a pull request (ADR 0061). Disabled while nothing has changed.

home.document.submitCopied.defaultMessage: The change is on your clipboard. Paste it into the issue on GitHub.
